paras: The lynching of Jack Walker was the killing of a Black man at or near Brenham, Texas, on July 23, 1888. A wire report said he was lynched because he struck the wife of a German in a quarrel over a horse, and a Texas paper reported that several German citizens had been arrested as participants. Outside Texas the episode reached readers as a single line in weekly news digests printed in Wisconsin, Dakota and Chicago.

According to the wire report, Walker, described as "colored," had quarreled with a German over a horse and struck the German's wife. The San Antonio Daily Light gave a less certain version, reporting only a rumor "that a lady was struck by the negro." Its added clause, "who was a relative of the parties," does not make clear whether the woman or the victim was meant.

The wire digests dated the lynching to Monday, July 23, and placed it "near Benham, Tex." The Daily Light, in its Texas news column the next day, placed it "at Brenham" and said only that a Black man "is found lynched." Neither account described how Walker was killed, how many men took part, or whether he had been held by anyone beforehand.

The Daily Light reported that "a number of highly respectable German citizens" had been arrested, charged with being participants in the lynching. No report of an inquest, of an examination of the arrested men, or of an indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

The only Texas report was one unheaded sentence in a San Antonio "State News" column, set among items on cotton, fires and a barbecue shooting, and it gave no name for the dead man. Its description of the arrested men as "highly respectable" was the only characterization of the accused lynchers in any of the papers.

The named version came from a national news digest that ran almost word for word in the River Falls Journal on July 26, the Kenosha Telegraph and the Big Stone City Herald on July 27, and the Chicago Citizen on July 28. That line gave the blow to the German's wife as the cause of the lynching without qualification, and it did not mention the arrests. In each paper it appeared among dozens of brief items on fires, drownings, executions and conventions, with no headline of its own.

The two accounts differ on the place, "Brenham" in the Texas paper and "Benham" in the wire digests; the Daily Light, a Texas paper printed the day after the lynching, is the closer source on this point. They also differ on the grounds, since the wire stated the quarrel and the blow as fact while the Daily Light reported the striking of a woman only as a rumor.

bases: Both the Texas brief and the wire digest say a Black man was lynched, and A1 reports several men arrested as participants (A1, A2).

Walker was reported lynched for striking a German's wife (A2), and A1 reports that 'a number' of German citizens were arrested and charged as participants, indicating an unlawful killing by several men acting on an accusation (A1).

A Texas state-news column (A1) and a separately worded national digest (A2) agree that a Black man was lynched at or near Brenham/Benham, Texas, on or about July 23, though both are brief and differ on details.
